title: Memory Traces Back to the Origin
content_html:
Memory Traces Back to the Origin

Considering the principles of dependent origination and cause and effect, memory would in theory be intact and traceable back to the origin of the universe? Does memory — understood broadly as causal trace or continuity of conditions — remain intact back to the origin of the universe?

Dual Perspectives

Physics / Information Theory

  • Physical law: most formulations conserve information (e.g. unitary quantum evolution).
  • Present states encode, in principle, all past states — even if scrambled (Laplace’s demon; holographic principle debates).
  • Memory as trace: every interaction leaves an imprint, but entropy disperses it beyond practical recovery.

Buddhism / Dependent Origination

  • Nothing arises independently; every moment depends on prior causes and conditions (pratītya-samutpāda).
  • No “first cause” — even the Big Bang is part of a conditioned chain.
  • Memory as karmic seeds: past actions leave traces (vāsanā, bīja) unfolding across lifetimes (Yogācāra ālaya-vijñāna).

Timeline Metaphor

Physics Timeline

Big Bang state encodes initial conditions (quantum fluctuations).

Stars form → matter interactions leave thermodynamic traces.

Earth systems → chemical “memories” in rocks, DNA, fossils.

Brains evolve → neural memory emerges as local information storage.

Present universe: information conserved but dispersed (entropy).

Buddhist Timeline

No absolute origin; cyclic or beginningless causality.

Arising of worlds depends on conditions (karmic and physical).

Beings accumulate karmic seeds (storehouse consciousness).

Memory manifests as present experience conditioned by past actions.

Future unfolds as dependent on current causes (no fixed end).

Synthesis

Traces are never lost - every event conditions the next.

Reconstruction is limited - physics: scrambled by entropy; Buddhism: empty of permanence.

Memory is woven into causality not an isolated faculty of brains but a universal principle of continuity.
